title: Safety
goals: Call emergency services and give clear information: what happened, where you are and who needs help.
Use can, could and be able to to talk about ability and possibility in the present, past and future.
Describe what was happening at a moment in the past with the Past Continuous.
Tell a story with when and while, mixing the Past Continuous and the Simple Past.
Understand safety advice at home and at work, and name common hazards and safety equipment.
Read and write an accident report: who, what, where, when and what you were doing.

learn.title: can, could and be able to
learn.html:
We use can, could and be able to to talk about ability and possibility. Can and could are modal verbs: they have no -s and no -ing, and the next verb is in the base form. Be able to works in all tenses.

TimeFormExample
Presentcan / can't / am (is, are) able toI can call an ambulance. She isn't able to walk.
Past (general ability)could / couldn't / was (were) able toHe could swim when he was six.
Past (one specific success)was / were able toThe firefighters were able to save the baby.
Past (negative, one event)couldn't / wasn't able toWe couldn't open the door.
Futurewill be able toYou will be able to walk next week.
  • For one specific success in the past, use was / were able to, not could: I was able to find the exit.
  • In the negative, couldn't is fine for both: I couldn't find the exit.
  • Can and could are also used for polite requests: Can you help me? Could you call 911?

watch.wrong: She can to drive an ambulance.
watch.why: After can, use the base verb without to.

watch.wrong: I will can help you tomorrow.
watch.right: I will be able to help you tomorrow.
watch.why: Can has no future form. Use will be able to.

watch.wrong: The firefighter could save the child (one time, yesterday).
watch.right: The firefighter was able to save the child.
watch.why: For one specific success in the past, use was / were able to.

watch.wrong: He doesn't can find the first aid kit.
watch.right: He can't find the first aid kit.
watch.why: Can makes its own negative: can't. Do not use doesn't with can.

learn.title: Past Continuous
learn.html:
We use the Past Continuous to talk about an action that was in progress at a moment in the past. We form it with was / were + verb-ing.

FormExample
PositiveI was cooking at six o'clock. They were working.
NegativeShe wasn't wearing a helmet. We weren't looking.
Yes/no questionWere you driving? — Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't.
Wh- questionWhat were you doing at ten?
  • It describes the background or the situation: It was raining and the road was wet.
  • State verbs (know, like, want, have for possession) usually do not take the continuous form.

watch.wrong: We was waiting for the ambulance.
watch.right: We were waiting for the ambulance.
watch.why: With we, you and they, use were.

watch.wrong: What you were doing at nine?
watch.right: What were you doing at nine?
watch.why: In questions, was / were goes before the subject.

watch.wrong: I was cook dinner when the lights went out.
watch.right: I was cooking dinner when the lights went out.
watch.why: After was / were, the verb needs -ing.

watch.wrong: She was knowing the emergency number.
watch.why: Know is a state verb. It is not used in the continuous.

learn.title: Past Continuous vs Simple Past: when and while
learn.html:
We often use both tenses in one sentence. The Past Continuous is the longer action in progress. The Simple Past is the shorter action that interrupts it.

StructureExample
while + Past ContinuousI fell while I was walking down the stairs.
when + Simple PastI was walking down the stairs when I fell.
Two actions at the same timeI was cooking while my father was watching TV.
Two actions in orderWhen the alarm rang, everyone left the building.
  • When the sentence begins with when or while, we use a comma: While I was cooking, the phone rang.
  • While is usually followed by the Past Continuous. When can be followed by either tense.
  • One short, finished action is in the Simple Past: I saw the accident.

watch.wrong: I burned my hand while I cooked.
watch.right: I burned my hand while I was cooking.
watch.why: The longer action in progress uses the Past Continuous.

watch.wrong: While I was waiting for the bus, I was seeing an accident.
watch.right: While I was waiting for the bus, I saw an accident.
watch.why: A short, finished action uses the Simple Past.

watch.wrong: While they crossed the street, a car was hitting them.
watch.right: While they were crossing the street, a car hit them.
watch.why: The long action is continuous. The interruption is Simple Past.

watch.wrong: I was breaking my arm when I was a child.
watch.right: I broke my arm when I was a child.
watch.why: A single finished event uses the Simple Past.

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• 911, what's your emergency? — what the operator says first.
  • I need an ambulance. There's been an accident. — saying what you need.
  • My father fell and he can't move his leg. — explaining what happened.
  • It's at 24 Hidalgo Street, near the bakery. — giving the address and a landmark.
  • Is he awake? Is he breathing? — questions the operator asks.
  • Please stay on the line. Help is on the way. — what the operator says to calm you.
  • Don't move him. Stay calm. — basic advice until help arrives.
  • Watch out! Be careful! Look out! — warning someone about danger.
  • Is everyone OK? Does anything hurt? — checking on people after an accident.
  • I'd like to report an accident. — talking to a supervisor at work.

Use the Past Continuous with when / while, and could or was able to at least once. Opening: Last year, I saw an accident...

write.model: Last winter, my cousin Luis had a small accident at home, and I was there. It was Sunday afternoon. I was making coffee in the kitchen while Luis was changing a light bulb in the living room. He was standing on a chair when it moved, and he fell. I heard a loud noise and ran to the living room. Luis was on the floor, and he couldn't move his left arm. He was awake, but he looked very pale. I called 911 and gave the address. The operator told me not to move him, so I put a pillow under his head and stayed with him. Ten minutes later, the paramedics arrived. They were able to take him to the hospital quickly. Luis had a fracture in his wrist, but he is fine now. After that day, we bought a ladder, and we never use chairs for that job again.

write.model:
Hi Mr. Torres,

I'm writing to report a safety problem in the warehouse. This morning, while I was moving boxes near the loading door, I saw oil on the floor. It was very slippery. Two coworkers were walking near it when I noticed it, so I put a yellow sign next to the spill and called the cleaning team. Nobody was hurt, but someone could fall easily. I wasn't able to clean it myself because I didn't have the right equipment.

Can you please send a cleaner today? Also, I think we need more wet floor signs near the door. Thank you for your help.

Best regards,
Ana

reading.title: Accidents at Home
reading.intro: Read the article about safety at home and answer.
paragraphs: Many people think that home is the safest place in the world. In fact, a large number of accidents happen in the kitchen, in the bathroom and on the stairs. Most of them are small, but some are serious. The good news is that you can prevent many of them with simple habits.

Falls are the most common accident. A wet bathroom floor is very slippery, so it is a good idea to put a rubber mat next to the shower. Stairs are also dangerous when they are dark or when there are toys or shoes on them. Last year, a man in Guadalajara broke his wrist while he was carrying laundry down the stairs. He couldn't see the last step.

Fires and burns come next. Many kitchen fires start when someone leaves a pan on the stove and walks away. A woman in Puebla was talking on the phone when the oil in her pan caught fire. She did not use water. Instead, she covered the pan with a lid and turned off the stove. Because she knew what to do, she was able to stop the fire in a few seconds.

Children are also at risk. They are curious, and they can reach cleaning products, medicine and hot drinks if adults are not careful. Experts say that families should keep dangerous products on high shelves and use safety gates near the stairs.

Every home should have a smoke alarm on each floor, a fire extinguisher in the kitchen and a first aid kit. Check the batteries of your smoke alarms every six months. Make a list of emergency numbers and put it next to the phone. In Mexico, the number to call in an emergency is 911.

Finally, practice what to do. Talk with your family about two ways to leave the house in a fire. When everyone knows the plan, nobody has to panic while the emergency is happening. A few minutes of preparation today can save a life tomorrow.

a soft mat that keeps your feet from slipping
the part of the body between the hand and the arm
the cover of a pan or a box
wanting to learn or touch new things
a small gate that stops children from reaching the stairs
to feel so afraid that you cannot think clearly
